# sleep-watch

tells a bot when the machine went to sleep, and on linux also right before it does. a bot that holds money (a lightning node) must not just keep going after a sleep, cuz another device might have taken over in the meantime. so the bot should stop, and after waking up datashell should first check with the other devices before it starts the bot again. nothing uses sleep-watch yet, bots arent built

```js
const sleep_watch = require('sleep-watch')
const on = sleep_watch({ interval, limit })

on({ wakeup, sleep }) // start watching
on() // stop watching
on({ wakeup, sleep }) // start again

// right before the machine sleeps (where the system tells us, see below), the machine waits till it resolves (5s max)
async function sleep () { await stop_bots() }
// after waking up. gap = how long the process was frozen (ms), at = Date.now() when the late tick came,
// announced = false if sleep() didnt run before, so we missed the sleep and the bots might still be running
async function wakeup ({ gap, at, announced }) {
  if (!announced) log_a_warning_in_the_audit_log()
  restart_bots_after_checking_other_devices()
}
```

the options are `interval` (100ms) and `limit` (2000ms). a tick that comes more than `limit` after the one before counts as a sleep. `sleep_watch.detect_system()` says which system it runs on

## how it knows

- **after waking up, bare and node** (any os, only tried on linux so far, not browsers, `timer.unref()` doesnt exist there). a timer ticks every 100ms. while the machine sleeps the whole process is frozen, so the next tick comes way too late and `Date.now()` jumped. thats `wakeup`
- **before sleeping**, it depends on the system, each one is a branch in `SYSTEMS` in [index.js](index.js). only linux with systemd is done, the others are `// TODO` and only get `wakeup`
- **linux with systemd, bare and node**. systemd-logind sends `PrepareForSleep (true,)` right before suspend / hibernate and `(false,)` after waking up. we listen with `gdbus monitor`, and we hold a "delay" lock with `systemd-inhibit`, so logind waits for us before it sleeps (`InhibitDelayMaxSec`, 5s by default). when `sleep()` resolves we release the lock, after waking up we take a new one
- the lock is held by a `cat` that `systemd-inhibit` runs, so it goes away when we close its stdin, and also when our process crashes or gets killed (`kill -9` tested), it never blocks sleep forever

## what it cant do

- `wakeup` only comes after waking up, not before
- a big clock change, or blocking the event loop for longer than `limit`, looks the same as a sleep
- `sleep` needs `systemd-inhibit` and `gdbus` (linux with systemd). without them it quietly only does the time check. linux without systemd (elogind), mac, windows and mobile are still `// TODO` in `SYSTEMS`
- `systemctl suspend -i` ignores locks, an empty battery or pulling the plug sends nothing, and if the bot needs more than 5s logind sleeps anyway. in all these cases only `wakeup` notices (with `announced: false`), after waking up
- it starts system tools (with `bare-subprocess`), thats a powerful capability, so its only meant for datashell itself, not apps

## cli

`node lib/node_modules/sleep-watch/cli.js` prints what it found (system, platform, tools). `cli.js watch` watches till ctrl+c and writes every sleep / wakeup to `sleep-watch-report.json`, `cli.js watch suspend` also suspends the machine after 3s (linux with systemd). people on other systems can run it and send us the json

## tested

`node lib/node_modules/sleep-watch/test.js` freezes node and bare processes with SIGSTOP for 3s (looks the same as a sleep from inside) and checks the gap, that `announced` is false when no `sleep()` came first, that `on()` stops and starts again, and that watching alone doesnt keep a process running. `sleep` needs a real suspend, so its not in that test, for that run `node lib/node_modules/sleep-watch/cli.js watch suspend`
